turns.text: ok so robotics ran 3:30 to 6 in C7 today and im mechanical lead so i have to explain our drivetrain choice to the team tmrw. lucas and i settled on a gear ratio and i need to be able to justify it. can you explain gear ratios and torque, short version pls. im on my dads old desktop after polishing my essay for like 2 hrs and alarm is 6:50 lol

Short version:

- Gear ratio = driven gear teeth ÷ driving gear teeth. A 5:1 reduction means the motor spins 5 times for every 1 turn of the wheel.
- Reduction trades speed for torque. Wheel torque ≈ motor torque × ratio × efficiency (about 0.85-0.95 for a typical gearbox). Wheel speed = motor speed ÷ ratio.
- Higher ratio: more pushing force and acceleration, lower top speed, and less risk of stalling or tripping breakers when pushing another robot.
- Lower ratio: faster top speed but slower acceleration, and more current draw under load.
- Pushing force at the wheel = wheel torque ÷ wheel radius, capped by traction (weight × friction coefficient). Past that point extra torque just spins the wheels.

If you tell me the motor type, wheel diameter, robot weight and the ratio you and your teammate chose, I can run the numbers to justify it.

ok. 4 motors total, wheels are 4 in diameter, robot is about 120 lbs, and the ratio we picked is 8.45:1. lucas wanted that. i want my math to beat whatever he came up with lol. he said it gets like 12 ft/s. can i get a better argument than just 'lucas said so'

Yes. I don't know your motor model, so I'll use [free speed] as a placeholder and show the method with a typical brushless FRC-style motor at about 5,600 rpm free speed.

1. Wheel rpm = 5,600 ÷ 8.45 ≈ 663 rpm
2. Wheel circumference = π × 4 in ≈ 12.57 in ≈ 1.05 ft
3. Free speed = 663 × 1.05 ÷ 60 ≈ 11.6 ft/s. Real loaded speed is lower, around 10 ft/s, so that matches Lucas's number as a ceiling, not a true cruising speed.

Traction check: 120 lbs × a friction coefficient of about 1.0 gives roughly 120 lbf of max pushing force. At 8.45:1 with 4 motors you'll have more torque than the wheels can use, so traction is the limit, not the gearbox. That's the argument for it: you reach the traction limit without giving up much speed, so it's a balanced choice.

To beat his case, test one alternative, such as 7.5:1, and compare speed and acceleration. If the gain is marginal, say so and defend 8.45:1 on traction and current draw. Send me your motor model and I'll swap in the real numbers.
ok that helps. so the argument is traction limited so more ratio doesnt help. ok bye
Exactly. Once you're at the traction limit, extra reduction costs you speed and gains no pushing force. Good luck at the team meeting, and get some sleep.
